cards.topic: Ch. IV — Sale I: Characterisation
cards.front: What is EMPTIO VENDITIO, and why does it have a double name?
cards.back:
A consensual contract in which the parties agree to exchange goods for money.
• The sources call it either EMPTIO or VENDITIO.
• EMPTIO = seen from the buyer's side (EMPTOR); VENDITIO = from the seller's side (VENDITOR).

cards.topic: Ch. IV — Sale I: Characterisation
cards.front: Why is EMPTIO VENDITIO a synallagmatic contract?
cards.back:
Both parties are necessarily bound; each is debtor and creditor of the other, and binds himself to get the other's performance.
• Buyer owes the price and is owed the goods — and vice versa.
• Principle DO UT DES: "I give so that you may give".

cards.topic: Ch. IV — Sale I: Characterisation
cards.front: What are the ESSENTIALIA NEGOTII of a sale, and what form is needed?
cards.back:
The indispensable terms the parties must at least agree on: the goods sold and the price.
• Consensual contract: obligations arise from bare CONSENSUS; no form required.
• Neither payment of the price nor delivery of the goods is needed to conclude it.

cards.topic: Ch. IV — Sale I: Characterisation
cards.front: Conclusion of a sale vs its performance — how does Example 12 (Lucius sells Melitta a gold necklace) show the difference?
cards.back:
Sale concluded 15 January (consensus on necklace and price 100): both obligations arise then; performed and extinguished 16 January.
• The obligations created by the sale ≠ their performance.
• Cash purchase: creation and performance almost coincide.

cards.topic: Ch. IV — Sale I: Characterisation
cards.front: Example 12 variant: on 16 January Melitta's slave is robbed on the way to pay; she no longer wants the necklace. Is she still bound?
cards.back:
Yes — the sale was concluded on 15 January; her obligation to pay arose validly and continues.
• Consensual creation: later events may make the deal unattractive but do not undo it.
• Not a "case of impossibility": the impossibility is subsequent and only subjective (p. 97).

cards.topic: Ch. IV — Sale I: Characterisation
cards.front: Which duties does EMPTIO VENDITIO include besides delivering the goods and paying the price?
cards.back:
Various subsidiary duties of disclosure, protection and care.
• Seller must not culpably damage or destroy sold-but-undelivered goods.
• He must warn the buyer of dangerous properties of the goods.
• He must answer for contractually stipulated qualities (warranty for defects as to quality).

cards.topic: Ch. IV — Sale I: Characterisation
cards.front: ACTIO EMPTI vs ACTIO VENDITI — who sues whom?
cards.back:
The buyer sues the seller with the ACTIO EMPTI; the seller sues the buyer with the ACTIO VENDITI.
• Both are BONAE FIDEI IUDICIA.
• Formula: QUOD DARE FACERE OPORTET EX FIDE BONA — no list of obligations.
• The IUDEX determines in each case what is owed; he has leeway.

cards.topic: Ch. IV — Sale I: Characterisation
cards.front: Property link: BONA FIDES in contract law vs BONA FIDES in property law — what is the difference?
cards.back:
Contract law: the standard of honest, fair dealing between contracting parties; property law: the acquirer's unawareness that the transferor was unauthorised.
• Contract sense: "good faith", basic standards of business integrity.
• Property sense matters for USUCAPIO by a buyer from a non-owner.
• It can occasionally matter in obligations too, eg seller unaware of a quality defect.

cards.topic: Ch. IV — Sale I: Characterisation
cards.front: What are NATURALIA NEGOTII?
cards.back: Rules arising from BONA FIDES where the parties agreed nothing express; fixed by the IUDEX and the jurists' opinions.

cards.topic: Ch. IV — Sale I: Characterisation
cards.front: What does ID QUOD ACTUM EST mean for interpreting a sale?
cards.back:
What the parties agreed — the chief source of their rights and duties.
• Narrow sense: what they expressly said or intended.
• Wider sense: what parties typically agree on for this type of contract.
• Also their hypothetical will: what they would have agreed, knowing certain facts.
• Ulpian D 19.1.11.1: nothing fits good faith better than performing what was agreed.

cards.topic: Ch. IV — Sale I: Characterisation
cards.front: Property link: does concluding a sale make the buyer owner of the goods?
cards.back:
No — the sale only creates obligations; ownership passes by a separate conveyance, usually TRADITIO (or MANCIPATIO / IN IURE CESSIO).
• Sale = the IUSTA CAUSA TRADITIONIS (legal ground) for the transfer.
• TRADITIO needs: transferor's authority, transfer of possession, IUSTA CAUSA.
• Necklace (Example 12): sale on 15 January, delivery on 16 January.

cards.topic: Ch. IV — Sale I: Characterisation
cards.front: Property link: a RES MANCIPI (eg a slave or an Italian estate) is sold — how does the buyer become civil-law owner?
cards.back:
By MANCIPATIO (or IN IURE CESSIO); a mere TRADITIO gives only bonitarian ownership until USUCAPIO.
• RES MANCIPI: Italian land, slaves, draft and pack animals (cattle, horses, mules, donkeys).
• USUCAPIO cures the form defect: one year (movables) or two years (land).
• Bonitarian owner sues with ACTIO PUBLICIANA; quirite owner with REI VINDICATIO.

cards.topic: Ch. IV — Sale I: Consensus and error
cards.front: Consensus in Roman law vs modern law — agreement of intents or of declarations?
cards.back:
Roman law stresses agreement of the actual intents; modern law looks at matching declarations.
• Modern: consensus if one party understood the other's declaration as matching his own intent.
• Provided that (mis)understanding was consistent with basic standards of fair dealing.

cards.topic: Ch. IV — Sale I: Consensus and error
cards.front: What is open dissent? (Example 13: Agatha offers a vase for 50, Tiro answers he will buy it for 40)
cards.back:
The parties want different things and say so openly — even the declarations do not match → no consensus.
• If Tiro merely misspoke and really meant 50 → consensus; sale at 50.
• In Roman law the agreement of intents is decisive.

cards.topic: Ch. IV — Sale I: Consensus and error
cards.front: FALSA DEMONSTRATIO NON NOCET — meaning and Example 14?
cards.back:
A false description does no harm: if both parties mean the same thing under a wrong name or price, the contract arises as intended.
• Example 14: "Fundus Sempronianus" named, both mean Fundus Cornelianus → sale of the Cornelianus.
• Cf Ulpian D 18.1.9.1 (Case 75).

cards.topic: Ch. IV — Sale I: Consensus and error
cards.front: Hidden dissent vs error — what is the difference?
cards.back:
Hidden dissent: declarations match, intentions do not; error: a party's declaration by mistake does not reflect his real intent.
• Example 15: each party means a different slave "Stichus" (cf Paulus D 45.1.83.1, Case 39).
• Example 16: Vibia accepts the Fundus Sempronianus but means the Fundus Cornelianus.
• Neither is visible to an outsider at first.

cards.topic: Ch. IV — Sale I: Consensus and error
cards.front: What is the Roman consequence of an error on an essential point, and which points are essential?
cards.back:
No sufficient consensus → no sale and no mutual obligations.
• Essential: type of contract, object(s) of purchase, price (cf Ulpian D 18.1.9 pr, Case 75).

cards.topic: Ch. IV — Sale I: Consensus and error
cards.front: Error on essential terms: modern Austrian law vs Roman law?
cards.back:
Austria: contract not void — it can be challenged if the mistaken party deserves protection, and exists until challenged. Rome: no contract.
• Defective goods (Austria): buyer chooses between challenging and keeping the contract.
• Keeping it: warranty — repair, supply of missing parts, price reduction.

cards.topic: Ch. IV — Sale I: Consensus and error
cards.front: What is ERROR IN NEGOTIO? (Example 17: Gaia and Pluto, a statue)
cards.back:
Error as to the type of transaction → no consensus, no contract.
• Example 17: Gaia offers to sell a statue; Pluto accepts, believing she lends it.

cards.topic: Ch. IV — Sale I: Consensus and error
cards.front: What is ERROR IN OBIECTO (ERROR IN CORPORE)?
cards.back:
Error as to the identity of the object: declaring for one object while meaning another → no sale.
• Example 16: Vibia declares for the Fundus Sempronianus but wants the Fundus Cornelianus.

cards.topic: Ch. IV — Sale I: Consensus and error
cards.front: What is ERROR IN SUBSTANTIA, and why is it controversial?
cards.back:
Error about the attributes or material (substance) of the object, not its identity; jurists disagree whether it voids the sale.
• At least some jurists: no sale where substance is wholly different — copper as gold, lead as silver.
• ERROR IN SEXU (about a slave's sex) also prevents a sale.

cards.topic: Ch. IV — Sale I: Consensus and error
cards.front: Why might the jurists have disagreed about ERROR IN SUBSTANTIA (philosophical background)?
cards.back:
Possibly divergent views on a thing's "essence" — parallel to the debate on specification.
• Aristotelian influence: essence lies in outward FORM → consensus on form suffices.
• Stoic influence: essence lies in SUBSTANCE → substance must match what was agreed.

cards.topic: Ch. IV — Sale I: Consensus and error
cards.front: Ulpianus D 18.1.9.2 (Case 75): A sells B wine; it turns out to be vinegar. Marcellus vs Ulpian?
cards.back:
Marcellus: sale valid — they agreed on the object (eg a particular amphora's contents). Ulpian distinguishes.
• Ulpian: wine gone sour = practically the same substance → valid.
• Ulpian: liquid that was always vinegar = different substance → no valid sale.

cards.topic: Ch. IV — Sale I: Consensus and error
cards.front: Ulpianus D 18.1.11.1 (Case 76): a female slave is sold — buyer believes (1) she is a virgin, she is not; (2) she is a boy. Valid?
cards.back:
(2) ERROR IN SEXU → no contract of sale; (1) no ERROR IN SEXU → sale valid.
• Variant 1: buyer gets a warranty claim for defect as to quality (Ulpian D 19.1.11.5, Case 121).

cards.topic: Ch. IV — Sale I: Consensus and error
cards.front: Julianus D 18.1.41.1 (Case 77): a table both parties believe solid silver is only silver-plated. Sale?
cards.back:
Julian: no contract of sale arises.
• Error relevant even though the material differs only partly.
• Julian goes furthest of the three positions.

cards.topic: Ch. IV — Sale I: Consensus and error
cards.front: Ulpianus D 18.1.14 (Case 78): co-heirs sell one heir jewellery all believe solid gold; it is mostly bronze. Sale?
cards.back:
Ulpian: sale valid — the item does contain some gold.
• Substances not completely different → no relevant ERROR IN SUBSTANTIA.

cards.topic: Ch. IV — Sale I: Consensus and error
cards.front: ERROR IN SUBSTANTIA: what are the three positions of Marcellus, Ulpian and Julian?
cards.back:
Marcellus: irrelevant; Ulpian: relevant only if substances are completely different; Julian: relevant even if material differs only partly.
• Marcellus: consensus on outward appearance decides (wine/vinegar, Case 75).
• Ulpian: sour wine, non-virgin, part-gold jewellery → valid (Cases 75, 76, 78).
• Julian: silver-plated table sold as solid silver → no sale (Case 77).

cards.topic: Ch. IV — Sale I: Consensus and error
cards.front: ERROR IN SUBSTANTIA vs defect as to quality — consequences and borderline?
cards.back:
ERROR IN SUBSTANTIA excludes consensus (no sale); a quality defect leaves the sale valid and gives the buyer a warranty claim.
• Quality defect: material defect impairing proper or expressly agreed use.
• Gold-plated table sold as solid gold: either no consensus, or valid sale with quality defect.
• If defect: buyer need not accept defective performance; may sometimes withdraw.
• Jurists affirming a sale despite ERROR IN SUBSTANTIA protect the buyer by warranty.

cards.topic: Ch. IV — Sale I: Consensus and error
cards.front: VIS and METUS under IUS CIVILE: is a coerced transaction valid, and how is the coerced party protected?
cards.back:
In principle valid — Paulus D 4.2.21.5: COACTUS TAMEN VOLUI (though coerced, I still willed). Praetorian remedies protect him.
• Sued for performance → EXCEPTIO METUS.
• Already performed → RESTITUTIO IN INTEGRUM: removing the effects of the legal act.
• Restoration mainly via ACTIO QUOD METUS CAUSA or EXCEPTIO QUOD METUS.

cards.topic: Ch. IV — Sale I: Consensus and error
cards.front: Coercion, fear and DOLUS MALUS: IUDICIUM STRICTI IURIS vs BONAE FIDEI IUDICIUM (eg EMPTIO VENDITIO)?
cards.back:
STRICTI IURIS: defendant must ask the praetor for EXCEPTIO METUS / EXCEPTIO DOLI; BONAE FIDEI: the IUDEX considers them of his own accord.
• Coercion and DOLUS contradict BONA FIDES → no obligation EX BONA FIDE for the victim.
• Covers coercion by the claimant or by a third party.

cards.topic: Ch. IV — Sale I: Consensus and error
cards.front: Exercise 17: Kassandra buys 50 litres of wine in an amphora from Leo. At delivery (a) it is olive oil; (b) the wine had already soured. Sale?
cards.back:
(a) Ulpian: completely different substance → no sale; Marcellus: valid if they agreed on the amphora's contents. (b) Soured wine: valid (Case 75).
• (b) Ulpian: sour wine is practically the same substance; Marcellus agrees in result.

cards.topic: Ch. IV — Sale I: Purchase price
cards.front: Which requirements must the purchase price meet?
cards.back:
It must be in money, seriously meant (PRETIUM VERUM) and clearly defined (PRETIUM CERTUM).
• No consensus on goods-for-money → no sale (another contract may arise).
• PRETIUM IUSTUM: not required in classical law; post-classical LAESIO ENORMIS.

cards.topic: Ch. IV — Sale I: Purchase price
cards.front: Paulus D 18.1.1.1 (Case 52): A is to give B a toga and receive a tunica in return. Sale?
cards.back:
Nerva and Proculus (Paulus agrees): no sale — one cannot tell who is seller and who is buyer.
• It is barter, an innominate contract.
• Sabinian minority (Sabinus, Cassius): it is a sale.

cards.topic: Ch. IV — Sale I: Purchase price
cards.front: Pomponius D 19.1.6.1 (Case 53): E sells T a tenement house; T pays a fixed sum and promises to renovate another house of E. Sale?
cards.back:
Yes, EMPTIO VENDITIO; E has the ACTIO VENDITI against T for the renovation.
• Had the renovation been the only consideration → no sale.

cards.topic: Ch. IV — Sale I: Purchase price
cards.front: What is PRETIUM VERUM, and when is it lacking?
cards.back:
A seriously meant (real) price; lacking where the price is merely symbolic and the parties really intend a gift.
• Example 18: Leo "sells" the Fundus Sempronianus (worth 200.000) to Niobe for 1.
• PRETIUM SIMULATUM: agreed from the start not to collect the price → gift (Ulpian D 18.1.36, Case 58).
• Contrast: after a valid sale the seller may defer or waive the price.

cards.topic: Ch. IV — Sale I: Purchase price
cards.front: EMPTIO VENDITIO vs DONATIO: in Example 18, can Niobe sue Leo if he refuses to deliver the estate?
cards.back:
No ACTIO EMPTI: there is no sale, and an informal donative promise (not a stipulation) is unenforceable.
• DONATIO = gratuitous; contract law for non-gratuitous transactions does not apply.
• DONATIO only justifies the recipient keeping the gift.
• DONATIO is a valid CAUSA TRADITIONIS / CAUSA USUCAPIONIS.

cards.topic: Ch. IV — Sale I: Purchase price
cards.front: What is a mixed gift? (Example 19: Thetis sells her nephew Pausanias land worth 200.000 for 100.000)
cards.back:
A seriously meant price deliberately below value, with donative intent → still EMPTIO VENDITIO (cf Ulpian D 18.1.38, Case 59).
• Thetis gifts Pausanias the difference.
• Requires ANIMUS DONANDI.
• Rules for non-gratuitous transactions (eg warranty) apply only partially.

cards.topic: Ch. IV — Sale I: Purchase price
cards.front: Mixed gift between spouses — valid? What is AGERE IN FRAUDEM LEGIS?
cards.back:
Invalid: gifts between spouses are prohibited, and the ban cannot be circumvented through an "advantageous" sale.
• AGERE IN FRAUDEM LEGIS: keeping to a rule's wording while consciously subverting its purpose.
• Even a completed spousal donation lacks a valid CAUSA.
• Sale between spouses at the real value: unproblematic.

cards.topic: Ch. IV — Sale I: Purchase price
cards.front: When is the price a PRETIUM CERTUM?
cards.back:
When what the buyer owes is determinable by objective criteria — it need not be numerically fixed at conclusion.
• Example 20: statue "for 100 or 200" → no valid sale.
• Example 21: grain at 100 per metric ton → determinable by weighing.
• "What you paid" / "what I have in my coffers" admissible (Ulpian D 18.1.7.1, Case 54).
• "Whatever price you name" (one party's discretion): inadmissible (Gaius D 18.1.35.1, Case 55).

cards.topic: Ch. IV — Sale I: Purchase price
cards.front: Gaius Inst 3.140 (Case 56): goods are sold for whatever Titius estimates them to be worth. Valid sale?
cards.back:
Disputed: Cassius and Labeo — no valid sale; Ofilius and Proculus — valid sale.
• Supporters expect an estimate in the manner of a VIR BONUS — an objective criterion.
• Cf Proculus D 17.2.78: ARBITRIUM VIRI BONI is to be followed.

cards.topic: Ch. IV — Sale I: Purchase price
cards.front: Third-party price (Case 56): when is the contract formed on each school's view?
cards.back: Ofilius/Proculus: once parties agree on the object and on Titius as price-setter; Labeo/Cassius: only when (and if) they accept Titius' price.

cards.topic: Ch. IV — Sale I: Purchase price
cards.front: PRETIUM IUSTUM: classical vs post-classical law?
cards.back:
Classical: private autonomy — parties set the price freely; post-classical: fairness gains weight, gross non-equivalence becomes unacceptable.
• Classical: "naturally permissible" to buy something worth more for less (Paulus D 19.2.22.3, Case 60).
• Medieval scholars later build the doctrine of the "just price" on this.

cards.topic: Ch. IV — Sale I: Purchase price
cards.front: What is LAESIO ENORMIS, and where does it come from?
cards.back:
A seller who receives less than half the value of the goods may rescind the sale.
• Rescripts of Diocletian: C 4.44.2 (285 AD, Case 61) and C 4.44.8 (293 AD).
• Protects only the seller; buyers were protected by maximum-price edicts.
• Modern §§ 934 seq ABGB: any party in a non-gratuitous contract receiving under half.

cards.topic: Ch. IV — Sale I: Purchase price
cards.front: LAESIO ENORMIS: how does rescission work, and how can the buyer avert it?
cards.back:
Seller's unilateral declaration removes the sale as legal ground; the parties must restore what was performed.
• Buyer may prevent it by paying the difference up to the full value.
• He cannot be forced to pay it → FACULTAS ALTERNATIVA.

cards.topic: Ch. IV — Sale I: Purchase price
cards.front: What is a facultative obligation (FACULTAS ALTERNATIVA)?
cards.back:
The debtor owes one performance but may discharge it by rendering a different kind.
• UNA RES IN OBLIGATIONE, DUAE RES IN SOLUTIONE.
• LAESIO ENORMIS: buyer owes return of the item; paying the difference is optional.

cards.topic: Ch. IV — Sale I: Purchase price
cards.front: Exercise 21: Turia sells the Fundus Aemilianus to Solon for 80.000; it was worth 200.000. Classical vs post-classical law?
cards.back:
Classical: valid, no remedy — private autonomy. Post-classical: LAESIO ENORMIS — 80.000 is under half the value; Turia may rescind.
• Solon may avert rescission by paying up to the full value (120.000 more).
• He cannot be forced to pay: FACULTAS ALTERNATIVA.

cards.topic: Ch. IV — Sale I: The goods
cards.front: Purchase of specified goods (species) vs unascertained goods (genus)?
cards.back:
Specified: an individually determined object is owed; unascertained: a quantity from a class (GENUS), every item equally suitable.
• Example 22: Calenus sells "his vineyard" after joint inspection → specified.
• Example 23: "four hectares of vineyard in the Alban mountains" → seller may pick any.
• Not the same as non-fungible/fungible: that is objective (measure, number, weight).

cards.topic: Ch. IV — Sale I: The goods
cards.front: GENUS NON PERIT — meaning and limit (limited purchase of unascertained goods)?
cards.back:
"The category does not perish": performance stays possible as long as things of the class exist.
• Matters for possibility of performance and allocation of risk.
• Limited genus ("100 metretes of wine from my cellars"): impossible if the whole supply perishes.
• Dispute: did Roman law know only the limited, or also the unlimited genus purchase?

cards.topic: Ch. IV — Sale I: The goods
cards.front: What is an alternative obligation? (Example 24: Europa and Lentulus, sheep)
cards.back:
The obligor has two or more ways of performing, fixed as items or classes; the choice is typically his (Paulus D 18.1.34.6, Case 84).
• "The sheep Ara or the sheep Rando" → alternative obligation.
• "One sheep from my herd" → limited purchase of unascertained goods.
• The choice may also lie with the obligee.

cards.topic: Ch. IV — Sale I: The goods
cards.front: Alternative vs facultative obligation — and what if the owed performance becomes impossible without the obligor's fault?
cards.back:
Alternative: DUAE RES IN OBLIGATIONE; facultative: UNA RES IN OBLIGATIONE, DUAE RES IN SOLUTIONE.
• Facultative: obligor freed; no duty to render the substitute.
• Alternative: he owes the performance that is still possible.

cards.topic: Ch. IV — Sale I: The goods
cards.front: What is EMPTIO REI SPERATAE?
cards.back:
Purchase of a future thing (fruit, unborn slave child or animal), conditional on its coming into existence (Pomponius D 18.1.8 pr, Case 64).
• Condition precedent: if fulfilled, effective EX TUNC from the agreement.
• Neither party may prevent fulfilment; whoever does is treated as if it were fulfilled.

cards.topic: Ch. IV — Sale I: The goods
cards.front: Example 25: on 1 January Pharnakes sells Lysippe "the next calf born of my cow". Calf born 1 June / cow dies first?
cards.back: Calf born → condition satisfied, sale effective EX TUNC (as of 1 January). Cow dies first → condition fails, sale never takes effect.

cards.topic: Ch. IV — Sale I: The goods
cards.front: What is EMPTIO SPEI?
cards.back:
Purchase of the chance (hope) itself: a fixed price is owed whether or not the thing comes into existence — unconditional; buyer bears the risk.
• Eg a fisherman's catch sold in advance for a lump sum (Case 64).
• Under BONA FIDES the seller is probably obliged to try to realise the hope.

cards.topic: Ch. IV — Sale I: The goods
cards.front: EMPTIO SPEI vs EMPTIO REI SPERATAE — Examples 26 and 27 (Curius sells Helena next year's harvest)?
cards.back:
"Entire harvest for 50.000" → EMPTIO SPEI: Helena pays even if weather destroys it; "1.000 per ton" → EMPTIO REI SPERATAE: no harvest, no price.
• SPEI: object = an immaterial hope; unconditional; buyer bears the risk.
• REI SPERATAE: conditional; seller bears the yield risk.

cards.topic: Ch. IV — Sale I: The goods
cards.front: Exercise 22: Vibia promises Ufens 10.000 for all trophies his horse Olympia wins next year; it never wins. Must she pay? What if she bought "Olympia's next foal" for 2.000?
cards.back: Trophies: EMPTIO SPEI — she bought the chance and must pay 10.000. Foal: EMPTIO REI SPERATAE — price owed only if born.

cards.topic: Ch. IV — Sale I: Initial impossibility
cards.front: What is a "case of impossibility" (initial objective impossibility)?
cards.back:
Performance prevented by an impossibility that exists before or at conclusion (initial) and that nobody at all could overcome (objective).
• Thing perished before the sale → impossibility rules.
• Destroyed after conclusion → subsequent impossibility: passing of risk, defective performance.

cards.topic: Ch. IV — Sale I: Initial impossibility
cards.front: Objective impossibility vs subjective impossibility (incapability)?
cards.back:
Objective: nobody could perform; subjective: this debtor cannot, someone else could. Impossibility rules cover only objective impossibility.
• Paying the price is objectively possible as long as money exists.
• Melitta robbed (Example 12): subsequent and subjective → sale stays valid.

cards.topic: Ch. IV — Sale I: Initial impossibility
cards.front: Practical vs legal impossibility — examples?
cards.back:
Practical: the object never existed or no longer exists; legal: physically feasible but prohibited by law.
• Practical: a Hippocentaur; a library burnt down before conclusion (cf Paulus D 18.1.15 pr, Case 70/1).
• Legal: RES EXTRA COMMERCIUM; EMPTIO REI SUAE — buying one's own thing (Pomponius D 18.1.16 pr, Case 69).

cards.topic: Ch. IV — Sale I: Initial impossibility
cards.front: What are RES EXTRA COMMERCIUM, and can they be sold?
cards.back:
Things outside private legal dealings — their sale is legally impossible (cf Modestinus D 18.1.62.1, Case 67).
• RES PUBLICAE: Field of Mars (Pomponius D 18.1.6 pr, Case 65), a village market square.
• RES DIVINI IURIS: RES SANCTAE (city walls), RES SACRAE (temples), RES RELIGIOSAE (tombs).

cards.topic: Ch. IV — Sale I: Initial impossibility
cards.front: Property link: why is there no route at all for a private buyer to acquire a RES EXTRA COMMERCIUM?
cards.back:
It cannot be sold (legal impossibility) and cannot be usucapted — it is not a RES HABILIS.
• So neither the contract nor USUCAPIO can lead to ownership.
• The buyer can only recover the price (CONDICTIO INDEBITI) and reliance losses.

cards.topic: Ch. IV — Sale I: Initial impossibility
cards.front: Sale of a free man (HOMO LIBER) or a stolen thing (RES FURTIVA): when impossible, when valid?
cards.back:
Impossible only with the parties' knowledge: buyer knows the man is free; both know the thing is stolen. Otherwise the sale arises.
• Free man: Pomponius (Celsus) D 18.1.6 pr (Case 65); Licinnius Rufinus D 18.1.70 (Case 66).
• Stolen thing: Paulus D 18.1.34.3 (Case 68).
• Free man sold to unknowing buyer, freed in STATUS QUAESTIO → EVICTIO; presupposes a valid sale.

cards.topic: Ch. IV — Sale I: Initial impossibility
cards.front: Property link: must the seller be owner of the goods for a valid sale?
cards.back:
No — a sale of another's thing is valid (only subjective impossibility); but under NEMO PLUS IURIS his TRADITIO cannot make the buyer owner.
• Buyer gets possession and may become owner by USUCAPIO.
• Not for a RES FURTIVA: no usucaption (LEX ATINIA).
• Inheritance that is not the seller's: valid sale, buyer gets its value (Case 109/2).

cards.topic: Ch. IV — Sale I: Initial impossibility
cards.front: Legal consequences of initial objective impossibility — rule and exception?
cards.back:
Rule: the sale is invalid — IMPOSSIBILIUM NULLA EST OBLIGATIO.
• Exception: a buyer who trusted in the contract sometimes gets a claim against the seller.
• To base it on the ACTIO EMPTI, some jurists assume a sale exists.
• Not impossible: selling a future thing (REI SPERATAE) or a mere chance (SPEI).

cards.topic: Ch. IV — Sale I: Initial impossibility
cards.front: CONDICTIO INDEBITI — what is it, and what are its requirements?
cards.back:
Recovery of what was given by mistake to satisfy a non-existent debt — eg a price paid under a sale void for impossibility.
• A performance: conscious shift of assets from claimant to defendant.
• No legal ground (IUSTA CAUSA) for it.
• Mistaken belief that it was owed.
• IUDICIUM STRICTI IURIS for a CERTA RES or CERTA PECUNIA.

cards.topic: Ch. IV — Sale I: Initial impossibility
cards.front: Paulus D 18.4.7 (Case 109/1): A sells B an inheritance; after payment it turns out not to exist. Result?
cards.back:
No sale — the object does not exist; B recovers the price by CONDICTIO.
• Losses beyond the price are not recoverable with the CONDICTIO INDEBITI.

cards.topic: Ch. IV — Sale I: Initial impossibility
cards.front: Reliance damages vs expectation damages?
cards.back:
Reliance: losses from trusting in the contract's validity, avoidable by timely disclosure; expectation: lost benefit of performance, presupposing a valid contract.
• German: "negative" vs "positive interest" (cf § 878 ABGB, § 122 BGB).
• Impossibility: buyer gets price back plus reliance damages — not expectation damages.

cards.topic: Ch. IV — Sale I: Initial impossibility
cards.front: Examples 28 and 29: Leo hires an architect for land that is a RES RELIGIOSA; Ismene buys a temple vase worth 150 for 100. Which loss is which?
cards.back:
Leo's architect fees = reliance loss (recoverable); Ismene's lost bargain (150 for 100) = expectation loss (not recoverable).
• Both sales void; the price is recoverable by CONDICTIO INDEBITI.
• Timely disclosure would have spared Leo, but never given Ismene her bargain.

cards.topic: Ch. IV — Sale I: Initial impossibility
cards.front: Why must a seller disclose a known impediment to performance? What is CULPA IN CONTRAHENDO?
cards.back:
BONA FIDES requires (potential) partners to inform each other; a seller who knowingly stays silent acts with DOLUS.
• Today: pre-contractual duties of protection, care and disclosure.
• Breach = CULPA IN CONTRAHENDO (modern term).
• In contract law DOLUS = the opposite of BONA FIDES.

cards.topic: Ch. IV — Sale I: Initial impossibility
cards.front: Iavolenus D 18.4.8 (Case 109/2): A sells B (1) an inheritance that exists but is not A's; (2) a non-existent inheritance. Result?
cards.back:
(1) Valid sale — only subjective impossibility; buyer gets the inheritance's estimated value (expectation damages). (2) Only price plus transaction costs.
• (1) Seller's duty to perform turns into paying the money equivalent.
• (2) = initial objective impossibility.

cards.topic: Ch. IV — Sale I: Initial impossibility
cards.front: On which legal bases can a buyer claim reliance losses in impossibility cases?
cards.back:
Three constructions: an analogous ACTIO IN FACTUM, the ACTIO DE DOLO (if seller had DOLUS), or the ACTIO EMPTI.
• ACTIO DE DOLO: subsidiary, requires DOLUS MALUS, conviction brings infamy.
• ACTIO EMPTI: HOMO LIBER / RES FURTIVA — valid sale if buyer unaware.
• Other impossibility cases: sale denied, yet ACTIO EMPTI granted.

cards.topic: Ch. IV — Sale I: Initial impossibility
cards.front: Modestinus D 18.1.62.1 (Case 67): A buys land that is LOCA SACRA, RELIGIOSA or PUBLICA, believing it private. Result?
cards.back:
No binding sale, but the buyer has the ACTIO EMPTI for QUOD INTEREST, NE DECEPTUM ESSE — his interest in not being deceived.
• Justified as the seller's breach of BONA FIDES.
• Phrase need not mean the seller knowingly promised the impossible.
• Source of the modern term reliance damages.

cards.topic: Ch. IV — Sale I: Initial impossibility
cards.front: Do reliance damages require fault by the seller?
cards.back:
The sources leave it open: fault (concealing known impossibility, Case 65) or simply the buyer's loss through reliance (Case 67).
• Strict liability could rest on a seller's guarantee duty.
• Some jurists place possibility of performance in the seller's sphere of responsibility.

cards.topic: Ch. IV — Sale I: Initial impossibility
cards.front: Exercise 23: thief Victor sells Niobe's vase to unknowing Xerxes; after two years Xerxes sells it to Niobe for 100. Owner? Valid sales?
cards.back:
Niobe stays owner throughout. Victor→Xerxes: valid sale (Xerxes unaware); Xerxes→Niobe: EMPTIO REI SUAE, void — she recovers 100 by CONDICTIO INDEBITI.
• NEMO PLUS IURIS: thief transfers no ownership.
• RES FURTIVA cannot be usucapted (LEX ATINIA), despite two years.
• Stolen-thing sale void only if both know (Case 68).

cards.topic: Ch. IV — Sale I: Partial impossibility
cards.front: What is partial impossibility, and what decides its consequences?
cards.back:
Initial objective impossibility of only part of the performance; consequences follow the parties' original agreement (ID QUOD ACTUM EST).
• No interest in the remainder → like total impossibility (Example 30: circus twins, one dead).
• Divisible by the parties' will → rest sold at reduced price (Example 31: garden slaves).
• Key first step: economically total impossibility, or can the contract be adapted?

cards.topic: Ch. IV — Sale I: Partial impossibility
cards.front: Marcianus D 18.1.44 (Case 70/2): two slaves sold for a lump sum; one died before conclusion. Sale of the survivor?
cards.back:
No — no sale even for the survivor.
• Lump sum → parties treated both as one economic unit priced together.
• That unit cannot be delivered → economically total impossibility; whole sale invalid.

cards.topic: Ch. IV — Sale I: Partial impossibility
cards.front: Paulus D 18.1.57 pr (Case 70 a): K buys V's house; unknown to both it had burnt down. Nerva/Sabinus/Cassius vs Neratius?
cards.back:
Nerva, Sabinus, Cassius: no sale; price recoverable by CONDICTIO. Neratius: depends on how much burned.
• Major part burnt → buyer not bound, may withdraw and reclaim the price.
• Half or less → contract performed at a price reduced by the loss in value.

cards.topic: Ch. IV — Sale I: Partial impossibility
cards.front: Case 70 a: why do Nerva/Sabinus/Cassius see total impossibility, and what is the point of Neratius' threshold?
cards.back:
Old view: the house was the contractual main object, so the land alone is economically worthless. Neratius: a quantitative threshold for total impossibility.
• At least half standing → sale valid with price adjustment.
• He weighs both sides: only when most is gone may the buyer choose.
• Otherwise both parties remain bound.

cards.topic: Ch. IV — Sale I: Partial impossibility
cards.front: Property link: in Case 70 a the land survives the fire — why is it still total impossibility, given SUPERFICIES SOLO CEDIT?
cards.back:
In property law the house is only an accession to the land, but contractually ("I buy your house") the house was the main object.
• SUPERFICIES SOLO CEDIT: what is built on land follows the land.
• Land still deliverable, yet economically total impossibility (Nerva, Sabinus, Cassius).

cards.topic: Ch. IV — Sale I: Partial impossibility
cards.front: Neratius' partial-impossibility solution vs a defect as to quality — similarities and differences?
cards.back:
Similar: both concern flaws existing at conclusion; termination or price reduction, sale otherwise valid.
• Quality defect: spoken of only once the buyer took delivery and accepted the object.
• Impossibility question: only for defects stemming from initial objective impossibility.
• Seller's mere inability: possibly warranty, but contract not void.

cards.topic: Ch. IV — Sale I: Partial impossibility
cards.front: Exercise 24: Zenon buys a 1.000 m² plot for 100.000 and spends 20.000 on villa plans; part is LOCUS RELIGIOSUS. (a) 100 m²; (b) nearly three quarters?
cards.back:
(a) Partial impossibility, remainder suffices → sale of the rest at a reduced price. (b) Economically total impossibility → no sale.
• (b) Price back by CONDICTIO INDEBITI.
• (b) 20.000 plans = reliance loss: ACTIO EMPTI (Case 67), ACTIO IN FACTUM or ACTIO DE DOLO.
